blocks.text: The evaluation of a living kidney donor aims to ensure donor safety, minimize risks, and support informed, voluntary decision- making without undue pressure. The transplant program’s policies should guide the evaluation process. Both accepted and excluded donors require appropriate follow-up care plans.

blocks.text: Maintenance immunosuppression after kidney transplantation is critical to prevent allograft rejection and ensure long-term graft survival by using a combination of immunosuppressive agents tailored to balance efficacy and toxicity. The standard regimen typically includes a calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus preferred), an antiproliferative agent (mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine), and corticosteroids, with mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus or everolimus) reserved for special circumstances.

Monitoring schedule for the Kidney Transplant Recipients (Routine)

Kidney transplant recipients have high risk of getting complications including surgical complications (first 3 months), frequent infections (first six months) and complications related to immunosuppressive medications, including diabetic mellitus. Some of the immunosuppressive medications have a narrow therapeutic window and have toxic effects, including nephrotoxicity. Therefore, these patients need regular and frequent follow-up as indicated in the table below.

blocks.text: Baseline screening for HIV, HBV, and HCV is mandatory before transplantation to identify infection status and guide management.

For patients who are HIV-negative, HBV-negative, and HCV-negative at baseline, no routine serial viral load or antibody testing is recommended post-transplant unless new exposures, donor-derived infection risk, or clinical suspicion arises.
